gaps.text: outside supported scope: The enquiry asks for regulatory approval and for measurements on patients next month; the supplied material describes research-stage feasibility work on excised tissue and does not cover approval, clinical validation, sterility, biocompatibility or deployment timelines. A conditional shortlist for bench feasibility testing can still be given.

Combining several spectroscopy methods (data fusion) (Both methods must look at the same small tissue area and their data must be aligned to a common time step, because alternating separate probes cannot guarantee the same spot and the acquisition rates differ. Start from one classification model per method with block scaling or per-method scores, keep a separate calibration and diagnostic check for each instrument, and validate the fused model on held-out samples or patients. The fused model must beat the better single method, otherwise the second instrument is not justified.)
Regulatory approval or clearance status of any probe for clinical use.
Clinical validation, sterility, biocompatibility and disinfection requirements for intraoperative use.

items.finding: The source states that no clinical, ex-vivo, or in-vivo data are used or claimed, and that all quantitative results come from disclosed synthetic simulation for algorithmic demonstration only.
items.how_it_applies: This could inform the assessment by indicating that at least one intraoperative multimodal classification concept remains at a synthetic/conceptual stage, so clinical use next month is not supported by this source; it suggests a phased validation approach before patient studies.
items.limits_and_transfer_risks: The source is a conceptual framework using synthetic data and different modalities (NIR-DRS, HSI, elastography), not a Raman fiber probe or regulatory document; transfer to a surgical Raman probe and approval status is uncertain.

citation.quote: No clinical, ex-vivo, or in-vivo data are used or claimed; all quantitative results are generated by disclosed synthetic simulation for algorithmic demonstration only.
citation.label: E04 ¶3

items.finding: The source describes high-level data fusion as working at the decision level, where supervised models are first fitted to each data matrix.
items.how_it_applies: This could support starting with one classification model per method and combining per-method scores, as mentioned in the gap, before attempting tighter fusion.
items.limits_and_transfer_risks: This is a general process analytical technology review, not a tissue or intraoperative study, and it does not address spatial alignment or differing acquisition rates.

citation.quote: The high-level data fusion (HLDF) (also called "decision-level" fusion) works on a decision level. This means that the first step is to fit some supervised models to each data matrix.
citation.label: E02 ¶33

items.finding: The source notes that in some situations instrument complementarity was not sufficient to improve performance for several CQAs, citing a Raman and FT-IR food analytical study.
items.how_it_applies: This could inform the assessment by warning that adding a second instrument such as MIR ATR to Raman may not improve the fused model; the fused model should be tested against the better single method.
items.limits_and_transfer_risks: The cited example is a food analytical study with Raman and FT-IR, not intraoperative tissue or the same probe setup, so the result may not transfer.

citation.quote: In some situations, instrument complementarity (not data complementarity) was not sufficient to improve the performance of predictive several CQAs, as shown by a Raman and FT-IR data based food analytical study [73].
citation.label: E02 ¶36
